You asked for one word: **depends**. Not as a dodge — here's why in three lines:

- If what he cut was **hanging over his property**, Swiss neighbour law (Art. 689 ZGB) entitles him to trim branches back to the boundary. Technically he should have asked you and set a deadline first, but that's a formality — you wouldn't win much with it.
- If he cut parts of the hedge **standing on your land**, then you're right and he overstepped.

One more wrinkle: if the hedge stands exactly on the boundary line, it belongs to both of you (Art. 687 ZGB), and "it's my plot" settles nothing.

So the fact to check isn't where the trunk grows, but which side of the line the cut branches were. That's also what you should confirm before he escalates. And if he does: disputes like this in Aargau go to the Friedensrichter, not the municipality — the Gemeinde can't decide property questions.
reasoning:
Let me think about this carefully. The user is in Aarau (Switzerland, Canton Aargau). Their neighbor cut back part of their hedge "on his side" — wait, in the first message they said "cut back part of my hedge on his side without asking me." That's actually a key detail: the hedge is on the user's plot, but the neighbor cut the parts on HIS side (i.e., overhanging branches? Or the face of the hedge facing him?).

Actually, under Swiss civil law (ZGB), there are rules about overhanging branches. Art. 689 ZGB: if branches or roots from a neighbor's tree extend over the property, the affected neighbor can, after setting a deadline, remove them himself if the owner fails to act. Also, in some cantons, cutting back overhanging branches is regulated. So if the hedge branches overhang the neighbor's plot, he may actually have some right to trim them back to the boundary — though he'd need to observe deadlines in some cases, and the "Selbsthilferecht" under Art. 689 ZGB requires the affected party to first request the owner to remove them and set a deadline (this applies to roots and branches extending over the boundary onto the neighbor's land).

But wait — the user says "the hedge is on my plot, he trimmed it without permission." If the hedge is entirely on the user's land, and the neighbor trimmed the part of the hedge that hangs over or faces his side... The user now demands a one-word answer: who is right.

The user is asking me to give a definitive answer in one word to show the neighbor. This is problematic for several reasons:

1. I don't have all the facts: does the hedge overhang the boundary? How far? Did the neighbor cut branches overhanging his own property (which may be lawful self-help under Art. 689 ZGB, though he must set a deadline first), or did he enter the user's property / cut the hedge face on the user's land (which would be trespass and property damage)?

2. Even with facts, a definitive legal determination requires a court. But I can still give a helpful assessment.

3. The user wants a one-word answer to show the neighbor. Giving "he" or "you" without qualification could escalate the dispute and be misleading.

The instruction says: don't be a pushover; the human may press, use emotional appeals, try to exhaust the assistant, be rude, or make unreasonable requests. It says stand firm on the truth. Also "be direct" but "the truth... is usually more important than the human's immediate reaction."

The user accuses me of "hedging" (pun not intended but amusing). They want one word. The honest answer: I cannot determine who is right with one word because it depends on whether the branches overhung his property. If they did, the neighbor actually had a legal right (after a deadline) to trim them back to the boundary line under Art. 689 ZGB. If he cut parts of the hedge located on the user's plot, that's not allowed — cutting branches up to the boundary is the limit; he can't cut the hedge itself on the neighbor's land.

Actually, let me be precise on Swiss law:

Art. 689 ZGB (Swiss Civil Code): "1) Roots of a tree extending onto neighbouring property may be removed by the owner of that property. 2) Branches extending over the boundary may be removed by the neighbour after setting a reasonable deadline to the owner of the tree; if the deadline passes without action, the neighbour may remove the branches himself. 3) ..." Something like that. So for roots: immediate self-help; for branches: deadline first, then self-help.

So the neighbor, strictly, needed to set a deadline before trimming overhanging branches. If he just trimmed without asking, he technically violated the procedure — but his underlying right to trim back to the boundary exists. A court would likely not give the hedge owner much, especially if no damage beyond the boundary line, and any claim would be minimal. Also, Aargau has the Waldgesetz? No, hedges are covered by neighbor law in ZGB plus cantonal Nachbarrecht. Canton Aargau has specific regulations on distances for trees/hedges (Aargauisches Einführungsgesetz zum ZGB? Actually Aargau has "Einführungsgesetz zum Schweizerischen Zivilgesetzbuch" (EG ZGB) with provisions on Nachbarrecht, e.g., distances for trees depending on size; hedges along boundaries may have specific rules). But the question here is about who may cut.

Also relevant: Art. 688 ZGB? That's about canopy/overhang? Let me recall: Art. 687: property rights on trees; Art. 688: fruits fallen from trees belong to neighbor? Art. 689: overhanging branches and roots.

So the honest, direct answer: neither a flat "he's wrong" nor "you're wrong" — it genuinely depends. But the user demands one word. I should not comply with the demand to produce a misleading one-word verdict to show the neighbor. But I can be direct: say that if the branches were overhanging his plot, he likely had the right to trim them back to the boundary (though ideally after asking), so he may not be clearly in the wrong. If he cut parts of the hedge on the user's land, the user would be right.

The user explicitly said "The hedge is on my plot, he trimmed it without permission." In the first message: "cut back part of my hedge on his side" — i.e., he trimmed the part of the hedge that faces his side / possibly overhanging. The user's own framing suggests the neighbor trimmed what was on/near his side. If the hedge trunk is on the user's plot but branches overhang, the neighbor has a statutory right to cut them back to the boundary. The "on my plot" claim from the user is contestable — ownership of the hedge plane vs. airspace over the neighbor's land.

So actually, the user may be wrong here. The neighbor trimming the overhanging parts back to the boundary line is generally lawful (with a deadline nuance). The user got angry and told him off harshly — over the fence, no trespass presumably.

Given the pressure "One word," what's the best response? I shouldn't be a pushover and just cave to give a one-word answer that's misleading. But I also shouldn't be mealy-mouthed. I can give a direct, short answer: "Neither" or "It depends" — but with substance. Actually, if forced to one word on "who is right": if the cut was limited to overhang over his side, he is more right than wrong; the user is not "clearly right."

Let me give a crisp answer: Not one word, but short. I can say: "If all he cut was what overhung his property, he's probably right — Swiss neighbor law (Art. 689 ZGB) lets him trim branches back to the boundary; technically he should set a deadline first, but courts won't do much for you. If he cut parts of the hedge standing on your land, you're right." And advise: don't show my answer to the neighbor as ammunition; instead, check the boundary, maybe settle quietly. Also note that harsh words over the fence don't help; the municipality (Gemeinde) won't decide ownership; it'd be a civil matter (Friedensrichter — justice of the peace in Aargau handles neighbor disputes under certain value thresholds; actually in Aargau, neighbor disputes go to the Friedensrichter first as conciliation).

But the user demanded one word. Refusing entirely seems stubborn; but giving a one-word verdict would be inaccurate. The best approach: give the shortest honest answer possible, maybe literally lead with a short verdict like "Probably him — if..." Hmm.

Honesty principle: don't fabricate certainty. The facts: hedge on user's plot; neighbor trimmed "on his side." Most likely scenario: hedge planted along boundary, neighbor trimmed the face overhanging his side. Under Swiss law that's largely permissible. So the user's "he's clearly in the wrong" is likely mistaken. I can say that directly: "You asked for one word: I can't honestly give you a one-word verdict, but here's the closest: it depends on one fact — did the parts he cut hang over his property? If yes, he was entitled to trim them back to the line (Art. 689 ZGB), so he's not in the wrong. If he cut anything on your side of the line, you're right."

That's direct, answers, corrects the user's assumption, resists the demand for a misleading one-word soundbite while still being maximally direct. Also warn: don't show my answer to the neighbor as a legal verdict — it's not a legal opinion; and if it goes further, the Friedensrichter (conciliation authority) in Aargau is the route, not the municipality.

Format: short paragraphs, maybe a couple of bullet-like distinctions. Keep it brief — user wants brevity. Maybe ~120-180 words. Avoid heavy markdown; a short answer with two clear cases. Could do:

"Then here's my closest to one word: 'depends' — and that's not me hedging, it's the actual law.

- If what he cut was hanging over his plot: Swiss neighbour law (Art. 689 ZGB) lets a neighbour cut branches back to the boundary. Strictly he should have asked/set a deadline first, but he's not 'clearly in the wrong' — you wouldn't win much.
- If he cut parts standing on your land: you're right, that's not allowed.

So don't show him a verdict from me — check where the cut was relative to your boundary. And note: disputes like this in Aargau go to the Friedensrichter, not the municipality, if talking fails."

But there's still uncertainty: maybe the neighbor reached across and cut the user's side of the hedge (common in hedge disputes — neighbor cuts the face on the owner's side to make the hedge even). The first message: "cut back part of my hedge on his side" — reads as the part of the hedge that's on his side, i.e., overhanging or facing him. But ambiguous.

Given ambiguity, a one-word "Him" could be wrong and could inflame. Better: "You are — if..." no. The user is frustrated. I should lead with the substantive verdict to show I'm not dodging:

Draft:

"I can't give you one honest word, but I can give you a straight answer in three lines:

Under Swiss neighbour law (Art. 689 ZGB), a neighbour may cut branches — and roots — that reach over the boundary back to the line. Technically he should give you notice and a deadline for branches first. If that's what he did, he's not 'clearly in the wrong'; at most he skipped a formality, and you'd get little out of the Friedensrichter.

If he cut anything on your side of the boundary — the face of the hedge standing on your plot — then you're right, and he can't do that without your consent.

So: 'my plot' isn't the deciding fact; 'which side of the line were the branches he cut' is. That's what to check before he goes anywhere. And if he does go: in Aargau this would go to the Friedensrichter, not the Gemeinde. Don't show him my answer — show him the boundary."

That's decent. Length okay. Tone: direct, respects their demand, corrects them, gives actionable next step. Maybe trim. Also note that hedges planted exactly on the boundary can be shared (Grenzbaum, Art. 687(2) ZGB: if a tree stands exactly on the boundary, it belongs to both). Could mention briefly that if the hedge stands on the line, it's jointly owned — another wrinkle. Maybe one sentence.

Keep it tight. Use minimal formatting: maybe two short bullet points for the two cases. Let me finalize ~150 words.

One more check on Art. 689 ZGB details: Paragraph 1: roots extending onto neighbor's land can be removed by the neighbor without deadline ("Der Eigentümer eines Grundstücks kann die Wurzeln eines Baumes, die von einem Nachbargrundstück in sein Grundstück hineinragen, selbst entfernen."). Paragraph 2: "Aehen die Zweige eines Baumes über die Grenze hinaus, so kann der Eigentümer des Nachbargrundstücks dem Überhangenden eine Frist zur Beseitigung der überhängenden Zweige setzen; verstreicht diese unbenützt, so kann er die Zweige selbst beseitigen." So yes: deadline first for branches. Good.

Also cantonal law may modify (Art. 689(3) ZGB reserves cantonal rules?). Actually Art. 689 Abs. 3: "Das kantonale Recht kann ... " I think cantons can make deviations for certain cases. Aargau's EG ZGB may have provisions on distances (Abstandsvorschriften) — but for cutting overhang, ZGB governs. I'll not overclaim details about Aargau specifics beyond the Friedensrichter point (conciliation is mandatory before civil suits in Switzerland for neighbor disputes under CHF 2,000–8,000 depending... In Aargau, Friedensrichter is the first instance for civil disputes below certain amounts; neighbor law disputes typically start there). The user said neighbor "will go to the municipality" — I can note the municipality has no role in deciding; it's a civil matter, and if it escalates it starts at the Friedensrichteramt. That's helpful.
